ch15.anchor: he had been a tribute scholar
ch15.note: A gongsheng, or “tribute scholar,” was a senior licentiate of the Qing examination system, selected from the local district schools for advancement toward the imperial academy—a respectable standing just below the provincial (juren) degree. Liu Shaobai earned it, as the inscription says, in the dynasty's last examination cycle.

On 18 March 1926, troops of the Beijing warlord government fired on a crowd of students and citizens protesting foreign ultimatums, killing dozens; the writer Lu Xun called it “the darkest day since the founding of the Republic.”

Fu Zuoyi (1895–1974), a general who rose under Yan Xishan, won fame defending Suiyuan against the Japanese and chaired that province. In January 1949 he negotiated the peaceful surrender of Beiping to the Communists, and afterward served the People's Republic as minister of water resources. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: rescue Wang Ruofei, held in the
ch15.note: Wang Ruofei (1896–1946), a senior Party leader trained in France and the Soviet Union, was arrested in 1931 while working in the Suiyuan–Inner Mongolia region and held first at Guisui, later at Taiyuan; he was freed in 1937. He died on 8 April 1946 in the air crash at Heichashan that also killed Bo Gu and Ye Ting. Corroborated.
The clash at the Marco Polo Bridge (Lugouqiao) west of Beiping on 7 July 1937 that opened the full war between China and Japan; it is often called by its date, the “Double Seventh.”

ch15.anchor: Kang Sheng came to lead the land reform
ch15.note: Kang Sheng directed the 1947 land reform in the Shanxi–Suiyuan border region and became notorious for fomenting indiscriminate class struggle. Mao Zedong did move in early 1948 to correct the ultra-“left” line, as the text goes on to show. Corroborated, with the qualification that at the time Mao rebuked the leftist line in general rather than singling Kang out, and even praised aspects of his work.

Edgar Snow (1905–1972), the American journalist whose Red Star Over China—written after some four months among the Communists at Bao'an in northern Shaanxi in 1936, and published in London in 1937—first carried an eyewitness account of the Chinese Communists to the Western world. In its Chinese edition it appeared under the guarded title Random Notes on a Western Journey (Xixing manji). The “Pastor Wang” whose real name Snow would not print is identified in Chinese sources as Dong Jianwu. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: I still cannot disclose his true name
ch15.note: Author's note. Red Star Over China, Hong Kong: Nanyue Press, 1977 edition, pp. 22–23.

ch15.anchor: This pastor's true name was Dong Jianwu
ch15.note: Dong Jianwu (1891–1970), an Episcopalian priest trained at St. John's University, joined the Party in 1928 and worked as an agent of the Central Special Section under cover of the cloth. He founded the Datong Kindergarten, which took in the children of Communists—among them Mao Zedong's own sons, whom he kept until they were sent toward the Soviet Union in 1936, the same year he guided Snow into the Red base. His pastoral cover and intelligence role are corroborated in Chinese reference sources.

ch15.note: Author's note. My Life, p. 564. After the War of Resistance broke out, Pu Huaren served as a senior adviser to the 129th Division of the Eighth Route Army, as president of the Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu High Court, and as dean of the foreign-language college of North China United University; after 1949 he was president of the Beijing Foreign Languages Institute, a member of the Fourth CPPCC, and a standing member of the Red Cross Society of China. He died in Beijing on 15 January 1974, aged 87.

ch15.anchor: went every week to the mother of T.V. Soong
ch15.note: T.V. Soong (Song Ziwen, 1894–1971), the Western-trained financier and brother-in-law of Chiang Kai-shek, was the Nationalist government's finance minister and one of the most powerful men in Nanjing. His mother, whom Dong Jianwu attended at prayer, was the matriarch of the Soong family.

ch15.anchor: the British Concession authorities opened his trial
ch15.note: “British Concession” (Ying zujie) is the source's own loose usage: by this date Shanghai had no separate British concession, the British settlement having merged into the International Settlement in 1863. The court was the Settlement's Mixed Court. The author uses the older term throughout; it is kept as written.

ch15.anchor: forged "Notice of Wu Hao and Others Leaving the Communist Party"
ch15.note: This forgery, known as the “Wu Hao Incident,” was fabricated in February 1932 by Kuomintang investigators to demoralize the underground: “Wu Hao” was Zhou Enlai's alias, and Zhou had in fact already left Shanghai for the Jiangxi Central Soviet. The counter-notice described below, placed on 4 March through the French lawyer Baihe under the name Zhou Shaoshan, is a well-documented episode. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: was a well-known figure in women's work in Wuhan
ch15.note: Huang Dinghui, better known as Huang Mulan (1907–2017), was a celebrated woman of the Shanghai underground who lived to the age of 110; her part in the Wu Hao counter-notice is recorded in her own memoirs.

ch16.anchor: Sun Bingwen, Luo Yinong, Peng Pai
ch16.note: These were among the most prominent Communists put to death at the Longhua ground of the Songhu Garrison Command. Peng Pai and Yang Yin were shot there on 30 August 1929; Luo Yinong (1928), Chen Yannian and Chen Qiaonian, and others are counted among its victims, and Chinese memorial tradition honors the “Longhua Martyrs.” The scale of several thousand killed between 1927 and 1933 is the standard figure. Corroborated—with the caveat that for the 1927 dead Zhao Shiyan and Chen Yannian, non-PRC sources record the execution only as “in Shanghai.”

ch16.anchor: arrested by Han Fuju and sentenced to death
ch16.note: Han Fuju (1890–1938), the warlord governor of Shandong, was himself arrested and executed by the Nationalist government in January 1938 for abandoning Jinan to the Japanese without orders. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: What Chen Datong had said about the teacher-and-student tie between Jiang Fangzhen and Xiong Shihui was no lie.
ch16.note: Jiang Fangzhen (1882–1938), courtesy name Baili, was the foremost military theorist of Republican China and a former head of the Baoding Military Academy, where Xiong Shihui had been his cadet. The store officialdom set by such teacher-and-student ties is what Song Zaisheng turned to account. Corroborated.

ch16.note: “No. 76” was the collaborationist secret police of the Wang Jingwei regime, at 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai, set up in 1939 under Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun with Japanese backing; it ran interrogation cells and death squads against Communist and Nationalist agents alike. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: being a "diehard of the Yang Fan clique,"
ch16.note: The “Yang Fan clique” (Yang Fan sidang) refers to the 1955 purge of Yang Fan, director of the Shanghai public-security bureau, and of the intelligence veteran Pan Hannian. The campaign swept up many former underground and Special-Section operatives who had been employed in security work after 1949, recasting that employment as harboring counter-revolutionaries. Both men were imprisoned for years and posthumously rehabilitated in the 1980s. Corroborated.
